notes.meaning: News of the dried-up Jordan reached the kings of the Amorites and Canaanites, and their courage completely melted away. The flooded river had been their natural barrier against invasion, but God's miracle proved that the Almighty was fighting for Israel. When the living God goes before His people, even the strongest worldly powers are shaken.

God commanded Joshua to prepare flint knives and circumcise the men of Israel, renewing a sacred practice that had stopped during their wilderness travels. Circumcision was the physical mark God gave to Abraham to show that his people belonged to Him by covenant, which is a holy agreement. Doing this a second time did not mean repeating the rite on individuals, but restoring it for the nation as a whole.

Joshua obeyed the Lord immediately and circumcised the men at a place called Gibeath-haaraloth, which means the hill of the foreskins. Many leaders among the people likely helped perform the task so that it could be completed quickly. True faith shows itself in prompt obedience to God's word, even when the command is painful and humbling.

The reason for this mass circumcision was that all the fighting men who came out of Egypt had died during the forty years in the desert. That older generation had received the covenant sign in Egypt, but their lives ended in the wilderness because they had rebelled against the Lord.

While every male who left Egypt had been circumcised, none of the boys born during the long journey had received the sign. Their constant moving and the temporary suspension of covenant privileges left an entire generation uncircumcised.

Israel had wandered for forty years until the entire generation of fighting men died off because they refused to obey God's voice. The Lord had solemnly sworn that they would never see the fertile land promised to their ancestors, a rich land flowing with milk and honey. Disobedience brought serious judgment, but God remained faithful to His covenant promise to their children.

God raised up the sons of that fallen generation to take their place, and Joshua now circumcised them. They had remained uncircumcised all through the desert journey, but before they could claim the inheritance, their covenant bond with God had to be restored.

After the whole nation was circumcised, the men remained resting in the camp until their wounds were completely healed. Performing this rite inside enemy territory left Israel's army sore and helpless for days, which was a remarkable act of faith in God's protection. Because God had already terrified the Canaanites, no enemy dared to attack them while they recovered.

The Lord told Joshua that by circumcising the people, He had rolled away the reproach of Egypt. This meant silencing the Egyptian taunt that God had led Israel into the desert only to destroy them, and removing the shame of looking like uncircumcised slaves. To remember this deliverance, the site was named Gilgal, which sounds like the Hebrew word for rolling.

On the evening of the fourteenth day of the month, the Israelites celebrated the Passover while camped on the plains of Jericho. This feast remembered how God spared their ancestors from the angel of death in Egypt and set them free. Having now received circumcision, the people were fully prepared according to God's law to share in the sacred meal.

The day after the Passover meal, the people ate the produce of the promised land for the first time, including roasted grain and flat bread baked without yeast. The crops had either been stored in nearby barns by the Canaanites who fled into Jericho or gathered fresh from the fields. God faithfully supplied real bread from the soil He had promised to their fathers.

The miraculous manna that had fallen from heaven every morning for forty years stopped completely the day after they ate the land's crops. God gave the miraculous food only as long as His people were in the barren wilderness and truly needed it. When normal means of provision became available, God called them to eat and work like settlers in the land He had given them.

While Joshua was near the fortified city of Jericho, he looked up and saw a man standing before him with a drawn sword. Joshua boldly walked up to Him and asked whether He stood with Israel or with their enemies. The drawn sword showed that war had begun, not just by human armies, but by heaven itself.

The figure answered that He was neither friend nor foe in a human sense, but had come as the Commander of the Lord's heavenly army. Joshua immediately fell facedown to the ground in worship and asked what orders his Master had for him. By bowing and accepting commands, Joshua recognized that he was not in charge of this war; God Himself was leading the battle.

The Commander ordered Joshua to take off his sandals because the ground where he was standing was holy, and Joshua obeyed. This matched the exact command God gave to Moses at the burning bush in Exodus, proving that the same divine presence was now with Joshua. Joshua could go into battle with total confidence, knowing the Lord Himself was present to fight for His people.
